Note, The disciples of Christ must be more thoughtful how to <hi type="italic">do</hi> well than how to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> well; how to <hi type="italic">keep</hi> their integrity than how to <hi type="italic">vindicate</hi> it. <hi type="italic">Non magna loquimur, sed vivimus—Our lives, not boasting words,</hi> form the best apology. <div eID="gen22023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22024" type="x-p"/> (5.) <hi type="italic">When they persecute you in this city, flee to another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">v. 23</reference>. "Thus reject them who reject you and your doctrine, and try whether others will not receive you and it. Thus shift for your own safety." Note, In case of imminent peril, the disciples of Christ may and must secure themselves by flight, when God, in his providence, opens to <hi type="italic">them a door of escape.</hi> He that flies may fight again. It is no inglorious thing for Christ's soldiers to quit their ground, provided they do not quit their colours: they may go out of the way of <hi type="italic">danger,</hi> though they must not go out of the way of <hi type="italic">duty.</hi> Observe Christ's care of his disciples, in providing places of retreat and shelter for them; ordering it so, that persecution rages not in all places at the same time; but <hi type="italic">when one city</hi> is made too hot for them, <hi type="italic">another</hi> is reserved for a cooler shade, and <hi type="italic">a little sanctuary;</hi> a favour to be used and not to be slighted; yet always with this proviso, that no sinful, unlawful means be used to make the escape; for then it is not a door of God's opening. We have many examples to this rule in the history both of Christ and his apostles, in the application of all which to particular cases <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> and integrity are <hi type="italic">profitable to direct.</hi> <div eID="gen22024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22025" type="x-p"/> (6.) <hi type="italic">Fear them not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.26">v. 26</reference>), because <hi type="italic">they can but kill the body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.28">v. 28</reference>). Note, it is the duty and interest of Christ's disciples, not to fear the greatest of their adversaries. They who truly fear God, need not fear man; and they who are afraid of the least sin, need not be afraid of the greatest trouble. <hi type="italic">The fear of man brings a snare,</hi> a perplexing snare, that disturbs our peace; an entangling snare, by which we are drawn into sin; and, therefore, it must be carefully watched, and striven, and prayed against. Be the times never so difficult, enemies never so outrageous, and events never so threatening, yet need we not fear, <hi type="italic">yet will we not fear, though the earth be removed,</hi> while we have so good a God, so good a cause, and so <hi type="italic">good a hope through grace.</hi> <div eID="gen22025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22026" type="x-p"/> Yes, this is soon said; but when it comes to the trial, racks and tortures, dungeons and galleys, axes and gibbets, fire and faggot, are terrible things, enough to make the stoutest heart to tremble, and to start back, especially when it is plain, that they may be avoided by a few declining steps; and therefore, to fortify us against this temptation, we have here, <div eID="gen22026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22027" type="x-p"/> [1.] A good reason against this fear, taken from the limited power of the enemies; they <hi type="italic">kill the body,</hi> that is the utmost their rage can extend to; hitherto they can go, if God permit them, but no further; <hi type="italic">they are not able to kill the soul,</hi> nor to do it any hurt, and the soul is the man. By this it appears, that the soul does not (as some dream) fall asleep at death, nor is deprived of thought and perception; for then the killing of the body would be the killing of the soul too. The soul is killed when it is separated from God and his love, which is its life, and is made a vessel of his wrath; now this is out of the reach of their power. <hi type="italic">Tribulation, distress, and persecution</hi> may separate us from all the world, but cannot part between us and God, cannot make us either not to love him, or not to be loved by him, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Rom. viii. 35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">37</reference>. If, therefore, we were more concerned about our souls, as our jewels, we should be less afraid of men, whose power cannot rob us of them; they can but <hi type="italic">kill the body,</hi> which would quickly die of itself, <hi type="italic">not the soul,</hi> which will enjoy itself and its God in spite of them. They can but crush the cabinet: a heathen set the tyrant at defiance with this, <hi type="italic">Tunde capsam Anaxarchi, Anaxarchum nom lædis—you may abuse the case of Anaxarchus, you cannot injure Anaxarchus himself.</hi> The pearl of price is untouched. Seneca undertakes to make it out, that you cannot hurt a wise and good man, because death itself is no real evil to him. <hi type="italic">Si maximum illud ultra quod nihil habent iratæ leges, aut sævissimi domini minantur, in quo imperium suum fortuna consumit, æquo placidoque animo accipimus, et scimus mortem malum non esse ob hoc, ne injuriam quidem—If with calmness and composure we meet that last extremity, beyond which injured laws and merciless tyrants have nothing to inflict, and in which fortune terminates her dominion, we know that death is not an evil, because it does not occasion the slightest injury.</hi> Seneca <hi type="italic">De Constantid.</hi> <div eID="gen22027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22028" type="x-p"/> [2.] A good remedy against it, and that is, to fear God. <hi type="italic">Fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First, Hell</hi> is the destruction both of <hi type="italic">soul and body;</hi> not of the <hi type="italic">being</hi> of either, but the <hi type="italic">well</hi>—being of both; it is the ruin of the whole man; if the soul be lost, the body is lost too. They sinned together; the body was the soul's tempter to sin, and its tool in sin, and they must eternally suffer together. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> This destruction comes from the power of God: he <hi type="italic">is able to destroy;</hi> it is a destruction from his <hi type="italic">glorious power</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.9">2 Thess. i. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">he will</hi> in it <hi type="italic">make his power known;</hi> not only his authority to sentence, but his ability to execute the sentence, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom. ix. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> God <hi type="italic">is therefore to be feared,</hi> even by the best saints in this world. <hi type="italic">Knowing the terrors of the Lord, we persuade men</hi> to <hi type="italic">stand in awe of him. If according to his fear so is his wrath,</hi> then <hi type="italic">according to his wrath so</hi> should <hi type="italic">his fear</hi> be, especially because <hi type="italic">none knows the power of his anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>. When Adam, in innocency, was awed by a threatening, let none of Christ's disciples think that they need not the restraint of a holy fear. <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that fears always.</hi> The <hi type="italic">God of Abraham,</hi> who was then dead, is called the <hi type="italic">Fear of Isaac,</hi> who was yet alive, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen. xxxi. 42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.53">53</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The fear of God, and of his power reigning in the soul, will be a sovereign antidote against the fear of man. It is better to fall under the frowns of all the world, than under God's frowns, and therefore, as it is most right in itself, so it is most safe for us, <hi type="italic">to obey God rather than men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.19">Acts iv. 19</reference>. They who <hi type="italic">are afraid of a man that shall die, forget the Lord their Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12-Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.14">Neh. iv. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen22028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22029" type="x-p"/> (7.) <hi type="italic">What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">v. 27</reference>); "whatever hazards you run, go on with your work, publishing and proclaiming the everlasting gospel to all the world; that is your business, mind that. The design of the enemies is not merely to destroy <hi type="italic">you,</hi> but to suppress <hi type="italic">that,</hi> and, therefore, whatever be the consequence, publish <hi type="italic">that." What I tell you, that speak ye.</hi> Note, That which the apostles have delivered to us is the same that <hi type="italic">they received from Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. They spake what he told them—<hi type="italic">that, all that,</hi> and <hi type="italic">nothing but that.</hi> Those ambassadors received their instructions in private, <hi type="italic">in darkness,</hi> in the ear, in corners, in parables. <hi type="italic">Many things Christ spake openly, and nothing in secret</hi> varying from what he preached in public, <reference osisRef="John.18.20">John xviii. 20</reference>. But the particular instructions which he gave his disciples after his resurrection, concerning <hi type="italic">the things pertaining to the kingdom of God,</hi> were whispered in the ear (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.3">Acts i. 3</reference>), for then <hi type="italic">he never showed himself openly.</hi> But they must deliver their embassy publicly, <hi type="italic">in the light,</hi> and <hi type="italic">upon the house-tops;</hi> for the doctrine of the gospel is what all are concerned in (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 20, 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2-Prov.8.3">viii. 2, 3</reference>), therefore <hi type="italic">he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.</hi> The first indication of the reception of the Gentiles into the church, was <hi type="italic">upon a house-top,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.9">Acts x. 9</reference>. Note, There is no part of Christ's gospel that needs, upon any account, to be concealed; <hi type="italic">the whole counsel of God must be revealed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Acts xx. 27</reference>. In never so mixed a multitude let it be plainly and fully delivered. <div eID="gen22029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22030" type="x-p"/> 2. By way of comfort and encouragement. Here is very much said to that purpose, and all little enough, considering the many hardships they were to grapple with, throughout the course of their ministry, and their present weakness, which was such, as that, without some powerful support, they could scarcely bear even the prospect of such usage; Christ therefore shows them why they should be of good cheer. <div eID="gen22030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22031" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is one word peculiar to their present mission, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.</hi> They were to preach that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of the Son of man,</hi> the Messiah, was <hi type="italic">at hand;</hi> they were to pray, <hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come:</hi> now they should <hi type="italic">not have gone over all the cities of Israel,</hi> thus praying and thus preaching, before that kingdom should come, in the exaltation of Christ, and the pouring out of the Spirit. It was a comfort, [1.] That what they said should be made good: they said <hi type="italic">the Son of man</hi> is coming, and <hi type="italic">behold, he comes.</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">will confirm the word of his messengers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xlvi. 26</reference>. [2.] That it should be made good quickly. Note, It is matter of comfort to Christ's labourers, that their working time will be short, and soon over; the hireling has his day; the work and warfare will in a little time be accomplished. [3.] That then they should be advanced to a higher station. <hi type="italic">When the Son of man comes, they shall be endued with greater power from on high;</hi> now they were sent forth as agents and envoys, but in a little time their commission should be enlarged, and they should be sent forth as plenipotentiaries into all the world. <div eID="gen22031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22032" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here are many words that relate to their work in general, and the troubles they were to meet with in it; and <hi type="italic">they are good words and comfortable words.</hi> <div eID="gen22032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22033" type="x-p"/> [1.] That their sufferings were <hi type="italic">for a testimony against them and the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.18">v. 18</reference>. When the Jewish consistories transfer you to the Roman governors, that they may have you put to death, your being hurried thus from one judgment-seat to another, will help to make your testimony the more public, and will give you an opportunity of bringing the gospel to the Gentiles, as well as to the Jews; nay, you will testify to them, and against them, by the very troubles you undergo. Note, God's people, and especially God's ministers, are his witnesses (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">Isa. xliii. 10</reference>), not only in their <hi type="italic">doing</hi> work, but in their <hi type="italic">suffering</hi> work. Hence they are called martyrs—<hi type="italic">witnesses</hi> for Christ, that his truths are of undoubted certainty and value; and, being witnesses for him, they are witnesses against those who oppose him and his gospel. The sufferings of the martyrs, as they witness to the truth of the gospel they profess, so they are testimonies of the enmity of their persecutors, and both ways they are a testimony against them, and will be produced in evidence in the great day, when <hi type="italic">the saints shall judge the world;</hi> and the reason of the sentence will be, <hi type="italic">Inasmuch as ye did it unto these, ye did it unto me.</hi> Now if their sufferings be a testimony, how cheerfully should they be borne! for the testimony is not finished till those come, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.7">Rev. xi. 7</reference>. If they be Christ's witnesses, they shall be sure to have their charges borne. <div eID="gen22033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22034" type="x-p"/> [2.] That upon all occasions they should have God's special presence with them, and the immediate assistance of his Holy Spirit, particularly when they should be called out to bear their testimony <hi type="italic">before governors and kings; it shall be given you</hi> (said Christ) <hi type="italic">in that same hour what ye shall speak.</hi> Christ's disciples were chosen <hi type="italic">from among the foolish of the world,</hi> unlearned and ignorant men, and, therefore, might justly distrust their own abilities, especially when they were called before great men. When Moses was sent to Pharaoh, he complained, <hi type="italic">I am not eloquent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.4.10">Exod. iv. 10</reference>. When Jeremiah was set over the kingdoms, he objected, <hi type="italic">I am but a child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.1.6">Jer. i. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">10</reference>. Now, in answer to this suggestion, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> they are here promised that <hi type="italic">it should be given them,</hi> nor some time before, but <hi type="italic">in that same hour, what they should speak.</hi> They shall speak <hi type="italic">extempore,</hi> and yet shall speak as much to the purpose, as if it had been never so well studied. Note, When God calls us out to speak for him, we may depend upon him to teach us what to say; even then, when we labour under the greatest disadvantages and discouragements. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They are here assured, that the blessed Spirit should draw up their plea for them. <hi type="italic">It is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father, which speaketh in you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">v. 20</reference>. They were not left to themselves upon such an occasion, but God undertook for them; his Spirit of wisdom spoke <hi type="italic">in</hi> them, as sometimes his providence wonderfully spoke <hi type="italic">for</hi> them, and by both together they were manifested in the consciences even of their persecutors. God gave them an ability, not only to speak to the purpose, but what they did say, to say it with holy zeal. The same Spirit that assisted them in the pulpit, assisted them at the bar. They cannot but come off well, who have such an advocate; to whom God says, as he did to Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.12">Exod. iv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Go, and I will be with thy mouth, and with thy heart.</hi> <div eID="gen22034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22035" type="x-p"/> [3.] That <hi type="italic">he that endures to the end shall be saved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">v. 22</reference>. Here it is very comfortable to consider, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> that there will be an <hi type="italic">end</hi> of these troubles; they may last long, but will not last always. Christ comforted himself with this, and so may his followers; <hi type="italic">The things concerning me have an end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.37">Luke xxii. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">Dabit Deus his quoque finem—These also will God bring to a termination.</hi> Note, A believing prospect of the period of our troubles, will be of great use to support us under them. <hi type="italic">The weary will be at rest, when the wicked cease from troubling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.17">Job iii. 17</reference>. God will give an expected <hi type="italic">end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>. The troubles may seem tedious, <hi type="italic">like the days of a hireling,</hi> but, blessed be God, they are not everlasting. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That while they continue, they may be <hi type="italic">endured;</hi> as they are not <hi type="italic">eternal,</hi> so they are not <hi type="italic">intolerable;</hi> they may be borne, and borne <hi type="italic">to the end,</hi> because the sufferers shall be borne up under them, in everlasting arms: <hi type="italic">The strength shall be according to the day,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Salvation will be the eternal recompence of all those <hi type="italic">that endure to the end.</hi> The weather stormy, and the way foul, but the pleasure of home will make amends for all. A believing regard to the crown of glory has been in all ages the cordial and support of suffering saints, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16-2Cor.4.18">2 Cor. iv. 16; 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.34">Heb. x. 34</reference>. This is not only an encouragement to us to <hi type="italic">endure,</hi> but an engagement to <hi type="italic">endure to the end.</hi> They who <hi type="italic">endure but awhile, and in time of temptation fall away,</hi> have run in vain, and lose all that they have attained; but they who persevere, are sure of the prize, and they only. <hi type="italic">Be faithful unto death,</hi> and then thou shalt have <hi type="italic">the crown of life.</hi> <div eID="gen22035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22036" type="x-p"/> [4.] That whatever hard usage the disciples of Christ meet with, it is no more than what their Master met with before (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24-Matt.10.25">v. 24, 25</reference>). <hi type="italic">The disciple is not above his master.</hi> We find this given them as a reason, why they should not hesitate to perform the meanest duties, no, not washing one another's feet. <reference osisRef="John.13.16">John xiii. 16</reference>. Here it is given as a reason, why they should not stumble at the hardest sufferings. They are reminded of this saying, <reference osisRef="John.15.20">John xv. 20</reference>. It is a proverbial expression, <hi type="italic">The servant is not better than his master,</hi> and, therefore, let him not expect to fare <hi type="italic">better.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jesus Christ is our <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> our teaching <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> and we are his disciples, to learn of him; our ruling <hi type="italic">master,</hi> and we are his servants to obey him: He is <hi type="italic">Master</hi> of the house, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oikodespotes</hi></hi>, has a despotic power in the church, which is his family. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Jesus Christ our Lord and Master met with very hard usage from the world; they called him Beelzebub, the god of flies, the name of the chief of the devils, with whom they said he was in league. It is hard to say which is here more to be wondered at, the wickedness of men who thus abused Christ, or the patience of Christ, who suffered himself to be thus abused; that he who was the God of glory should be stigmatized as the god of flies; the King of Israel, as the god of Ekron; the Prince of light and life, as the prince of the powers of death and darkness; that Satan's greatest Enemy and Destroyer should be run down as his confederate, and yet <hi type="italic">endure such contradiction of sinners. Thirdly,</hi> The consideration of the ill treatment which Christ met with in the world, should engage us to expect and prepare for the like, and to bear it patiently. Let us not think it strange, if they who hated him hate his followers, for his sake; nor think it hard if they who are shortly to be made <hi type="italic">like him in glory,</hi> be now made <hi type="italic">like him in sufferings.</hi> Christ began in the <hi type="italic">bitter cup,</hi> let us be willing to pledge him; his bearing the cross made it easy for us. <div eID="gen22036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22037" type="x-p"/> [5.] That <hi type="italic">there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.26">v. 26</reference>. We understand this, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of the revealing of the gospel to all the world. "Do you <hi type="italic">publish</hi> it (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">v. 27</reference>), for it shall be published. The truths which are now, as mysteries, hid from the children of men, shall all be made known, to all nations, in their own language," <reference osisRef="Acts.2.11">Acts ii. 11</reference>. The <hi type="italic">ends of the earth must see this salvation.</hi> Note, It is a great encouragement to those who are doing Christ's work, that it is a work which shall certainly be done. It is a plough which God will speed. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of the clearing up of the innocency of Christ's suffering servants, that are called Beelzebub; their true character is now invidiously disguised with false colours, but however their innocency and excellency are now <hi type="italic">covered,</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall be revealed;</hi> sometimes it is in a great measure done in this world, when the righteousness of the saints is made, by subsequent events, to <hi type="italic">shine forth as the light:</hi> however it will be done at the great day, when their glory shall be manifested to all the world, angels and men, to whom they are now <hi type="italic">made spectacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1 Cor. iv. 9</reference>. All their reproach shall be rolled away, and their graces and services, that are now <hi type="italic">covered, shall be revealed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1 Cor. iv. 5</reference>. Note, It is matter of comfort to the people of God, under all the calumnies and censures of men, that there will be a resurrection of <hi type="italic">names</hi> as well as of <hi type="italic">bodies,</hi> at the last day, when <hi type="italic">the righteous shall shine forth as the sun.</hi> Let Christ's ministers faithfully reveal his truths, and then leave it to him, in due time, to reveal their integrity. <div eID="gen22037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22038" type="x-p"/> [6.] That the providence of God is in a special manner conversant about the saints, in their suffering, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.29-Matt.10.31">v. 29-31</reference>. It is good to have recourse to our first principles, and particularly to the doctrine of God's universal providence, extending itself to all the creatures, and all their actions, even the smallest and most minute. The light of nature teaches us this, and it is comfortable to all men, but especially to all good men, who can in faith call this God their Father, and for whom he has a tender concern. See here, <div eID="gen22038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22039" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The general extent of providence to all the creatures, even the least, and least considerable, to the <hi type="italic">sparrows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.29">v. 29</reference>. These little animals are of so small account, that one of them is not valued; there must go two to be worth <hi type="italic">a farthing</hi> (nay, you shall have five for a halfpenny, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.6">Luke xii. 6</reference>), and yet they are not shut out of the divine care; <hi type="italic">One of them shall not fall to the ground without your Father:</hi> That is, 1. They do not light on <hi type="italic">the ground</hi> for food, to pick up a grain of corn, but <hi type="italic">your</hi> heavenly <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> by his providence, laid it ready for them. In the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.6">Luke xii. 6</reference>, it is thus expressed, <hi type="italic">Not one of them is forgotten before God,</hi> forgotten to be provided for; <hi type="italic">he feedeth them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">ch. vi. 26</reference>. Now he that feeds the sparrows, will not starve the saints. 2. They do <hi type="italic">not fall to the ground</hi> by death, either a natural or a violent death, without the notice of God: though they are so small a part of the creation, yet even their death comes within the notice of the divine providence; much more does the death of his disciples. Observe, The birds that soar above, when they die, <hi type="italic">fall to the ground;</hi> death brings the highest to the earth. Some think that Christ here alludes to the <hi type="italic">two sparrows</hi> that were used in cleansing the leper (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.4-Lev.14.6">Lev. xiv. 4-6</reference>); the two birds in the margin are called <hi type="italic">sparrows;</hi> of these one was killed, and so <hi type="italic">fell to the ground,</hi> the other was let go. Now it seemed a casual thing which of the two was killed; the persons employed took which they pleased, but God's providence designed, and determined which. Now this God, who has such an eye to the sparrows, because they are his creatures, much more will have an eye to you, who are his children. If a sparrow die not <hi type="italic">without your Father,</hi> surely a man does not,—a Christian,—a minister,—my friend, my child. A bird falls not into the fowler's net, nor by the fowler's shot, and so comes not to be sold in the market, but according to the direction of providence; your enemies, like subtle fowlers, <hi type="italic">lay snares for</hi> you, and <hi type="italic">privily shoot at</hi> you, but they cannot take you, they cannot hit you, unless God give them leave. Therefore be not afraid of death, for your enemies have no power against you, but what is <hi type="italic">given them from above.</hi> God can break their bows and snares (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.12-Ps.38.15 Ps.64.4 Ps.64.7">Ps. xxxviii. 12-15; lxiv. 4, 7</reference>), and make our souls to <hi type="italic">escape as a bird</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.7">Ps. cxxiv. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">Fear ye not, therefore,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.31">v. 31</reference>. Note, There is enough in the doctrine of God's providence to silence all the fears of God's people: <hi type="italic">Ye are of more value than many sparrows.</hi> All men are so, for the other creatures were made for man, and <hi type="italic">put under his feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.6-Ps.8.8">Ps. viii. 6-8</reference>); much more the disciples of Jesus Christ, who are the excellent ones of the earth, however contemned, as if not worth one sparrow. <div eID="gen22039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The particular cognizance which providence takes of the disciples of Christ, especially in their sufferings (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">v. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.</hi> This is a proverbial expression, denoting the account which God takes and keeps of all the concernments of his people, even of those that are most minute, and least regarded. This is not to be made a matter of curious enquiry, but of encouragement to live in a continual dependence upon God's providential care, which extends itself to all occurrences, yet without disparagement to the infinite glory, or disturbance to the infinite rest, of the Eternal Mind. If God numbers their hairs, much more does he number their heads, and take care of their lives, their comforts, their souls. It intimates, that God takes more care of them, than they do of themselves. They who are solicitous to number their money, and goods, and cattle, yet were never careful to number their hairs, which fall and are lost, and they never miss them: but God <hi type="italic">numbers the hairs of</hi> his people, and <hi type="italic">not a hair of their head shall perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">Luke xxi. 18</reference>); not the least hurt shall be done them, but upon a valuable consideration: so precious to God are his saints, and their lives and deaths! <div eID="gen22040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22041" type="x-p"/> [7.] That he will shortly, in the day of triumph, own those who now own him, in the day of trial, when those who deny him shall be for ever disowned and rejected by him, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.32-Matt.10.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is our duty, and if we do it, it will hereafter be our unspeakable honour and happiness, to <hi type="italic">confess Christ before men.</hi> 1. It is our duty, not only to believe in Christ, but to profess that faith, in suffering for him, when we are called to it, as well as in serving him. We must never be ashamed of our relation to Christ, our attendance on him, and our expectations from him: hereby the sincerity of our faith, is evidenced, his name glorified, and others edified. 2. However this may expose us to reproach and trouble now, we shall be abundantly recompensed for that, <hi type="italic">in the resurrection of the just,</hi> when it will be our unspeakable honour and happiness to hear Christ say (what would we more?) "<hi type="italic">Him will I confess,</hi> though a poor worthless worm of the earth; this is one of mine, one of my friends and favourites, who loved me and was beloved by me; the purchase of my blood, the workmanship of my Spirit; <hi type="italic">I will confess him before my Father,</hi> when it will do him the most service; I will speak a good word for him, when he appears before <hi type="italic">my Father</hi> to receive his doom; I will present him, will represent him to <hi type="italic">my Father.</hi>" Those who honour Christ he will thus honour. They honour him <hi type="italic">before men;</hi> that is a <hi type="italic">poor</hi> thing: he will honour them <hi type="italic">before</hi> his <hi type="italic">Father;</hi> that is a <hi type="italic">great</hi> thing. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a dangerous thing for any to deny and disown <hi type="italic">Christ before men;</hi> for they who so do will be disowned by him <hi type="italic">in the great day,</hi> when they have most need of him: he will not own them for his servants who would not own him for their master: <hi type="italic">I tell you, I know you not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">ch. vii. 23</reference>. In the first ages of Christianity, when for a man to <hi type="italic">confess Christ</hi> was to venture all that was dear to him in this world, it was more a trial of sincerity, than it was afterwards, when it had secular advantages attending it. <div eID="gen22041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22042" type="x-p"/> [8.] That the foundation of their discipleship was laid in such a temper and disposition, as would make sufferings very light and easy to them; and it was upon the condition of a preparedness for suffering, that Christ took them to be his followers, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.37-Matt.10.39">v. 37-39</reference>. He told them at first, that they were <hi type="italic">not worthy of</hi> him, if they were not willing to part with all for him. Men hesitate not at those difficulties which necessarily attend their profession, and which they counted upon, when they undertook that profession; and they will either cheerfully submit to those fatigues and troubles, or disclaim the privileges and advantages of their profession. Now, in the Christian profession, they are reckoned unworthy the dignity and felicity of it, that put not such a value upon their interest in Christ, as to prefer that before any other interests. They cannot expect the gains of a bargain, who will not come up to the terms of it. Now thus the terms are settled; if religion be worth <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing, it is worth <hi type="italic">every</hi> thing: and, therefore, all who believe the truth of it, will soon come up to the price of it; and they who make it their business and bliss, will make every thing else to yield to it. They who like not Christ on these terms, may leave him at their peril. Note, It is very encouraging to think, that whatever we leave, or lose, or suffer for Christ, we do not make a hard bargain for ourselves. Whatever we part with for this pearl of price, we may comfort ourselves with this persuasion, that it is well worth what we give for it. The terms are, that we must prefer Christ. <div eID="gen22042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22043" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Before our nearest and dearest relations; <hi type="italic">father or mother, son or daughter.</hi> Between these relations, because there is little room left for envy, there is commonly more room for love, and, therefore, these are instanced, as relations which are most likely to affect us. Children must love their parents, and parents must love their children; but if they love them better than Christ, they are unworthy of him. As we must not be <hi type="italic">deterred</hi> from Christ by the hatred of our relations which he spoke of (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.21">v. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.35">35</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">36</reference>), so we must not be <hi type="italic">drawn</hi> from him, by their love. Christians must be as Levi, who <hi type="italic">said to his father, I have not seen him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen22043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22044" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Before our ease and safety. We must <hi type="italic">take up our cross</hi> and <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> else we are <hi type="italic">not worthy</hi> of him. Here observe, 1. They who would <hi type="italic">follow Christ,</hi> must expect <hi type="italic">their cross</hi> and <hi type="italic">take it up.</hi> 2. In taking <hi type="italic">up the cross,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">follow Christ's</hi> example, and bear it as he did. 3. It is a great encouragement to us, when we meet with crosses, that in bearing them we <hi type="italic">follow Christ,</hi> who has showed us the way; and that if we follow him faithfully, he will lead us through sufferings like him, to glory with him. <div eID="gen22044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22045" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Before life itself, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.39">v. 39</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that findeth his life shall lose it;</hi> he that thinks he had found it when he has saved it, and kept it, by denying Christ, <hi type="italic">shall lose it</hi> in an eternal death; but <hi type="italic">he that loseth his life for Christ's sake,</hi> that will part with it rather than deny Christ, <hi type="italic">shall find it,</hi> to his unspeakable advantage, an eternal life. They are best prepared for the life to come, that sit most loose to this present life. <div eID="gen22045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22046" type="x-p"/> [9.] That Christ himself would so heartily espouse their cause, as to show himself a friend to all their friends, and to repay all the kindnesses that should at any time be bestowed upon them, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.40-Matt.10.42">v. 40-42</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that receiveth you, receiveth me.</hi> <div eID="gen22046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22047" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is here implied, that though the generality would reject them, yet they should meet with some who would receive and entertain them, would bid the message welcome to their hearts, and the messengers to their houses, for the sake of it. Why was the gospel market made, but that if some will not, others will. In the worst of times there is a remnant according to the election of grace. Christ's ministers shall not <hi type="italic">labour in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen22047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Jesus Christ takes what is done to his faithful ministers, whether in kindness or in unkindness, as done to himself, and reckons himself <hi type="italic">treated</hi> as they are <hi type="italic">treated. He that receiveth you, receiveth me.</hi> Honour or contempt put upon an ambassador reflects honour or contempt upon the prince that sends him, and ministers are <hi type="italic">ambassadors for Christ.</hi> See how Christ may still be entertained by those who would testify their respects to him; his people and ministers we have always with us; and he is <hi type="italic">with them always,</hi> even to the end of the world. Nay, the honour rises higher, <hi type="italic">He that receiveth me, receiveth him that sent me.</hi> Not only Christ takes it as done to himself, but through Christ God does so too. By entertaining Christ's ministers, they entertain not <hi type="italic">angels unawares,</hi> but Christ, nay, and God himself, and <hi type="italic">unawares</hi> too, as appears, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.37">ch. xxv. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">When saw we thee an hungered?</hi> <div eID="gen22048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That though the kindness done to Christ's disciples be never so small, yet if there be occasion for it, and ability to do no more, it shall be accepted, though it be <hi type="italic">but a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.42">v. 42</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">little ones,</hi> poor and weak, and often stand in need of refreshment, and glad of the least. The extremity may be such, that a <hi type="italic">cup of cold water</hi> may be a great favour. Note, Kindnesses shown to Christ's disciples are valued in Christ's books, not according to the cost of the gift, but according to the love and affection of the giver. On that score the widow's mite not only passed current, but was stamped high, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.3-Luke.21.4">Luke xxi. 3, 4</reference>. Thus they who are truly rich in graces may be rich in good works, though poor in the world. <div eID="gen22049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That kindness to Christ's disciples which he will accept, must be done with an eye to Christ, and for his sake. A prophet must be received <hi type="italic">in the name of a prophet,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">righteous man</hi> in the name of a <hi type="italic">righteous man,</hi> and one of those <hi type="italic">little ones</hi> in <hi type="italic">the name of a disciple;</hi> not because they are learned, or witty, nor because they are our relations or neighbours, but because they are righteous, and so bear Christ's image; because they are prophets and disciples, and so are sent on Christ's errand. It is a believing regard to Christ that puts an acceptable value upon the kindnesses done to his ministers. Christ does not interest himself in the matter, unless we first interest him in it. <hi type="italic">Ut tibi debeam aliquid pro eo quod præstas, debes non tantum mihi præstare, sed tanquam mihi—If you wish me to feel an obligation to you for any service you render, you must not only perform the service, but you must convince me that you do it for my sake.</hi> Seneca.  <chapter eID="Matt.10"/> <div eID="gen22050" type="x-p"/>

entries.618590cd836d8f2609b7cc48bc57e79411619994: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13485"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.10.1-Matt.10.5">Mt 10:1-5</reference>. Mission of the Twelve Apostles. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.6.7-Mark.6.13">Mr 6:7-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.1-Luke.9.6">Lu 9:1-6</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25779" type="x-p"/> The last three verses of the ninth chapter form the proper introduction to the Mission of the Twelve, as is evident from the remarkable fact that the Mission of the Seventy was prefaced by the very same words. (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.10.2">Lu 10:2</reference>).<div eID="gen25779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13485"/><hi type="bold">1. And when he had called unto him his twelve disciples, he gave them power--</hi>The word signifies both "power," and "authority" or "right." Even if it were not evident that here both ideas are included, we find both words expressly used in the parallel passage of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.1">Lu 9:1</reference>)--"He gave them power and authority"--in other words, He both qualified and authorized them.<div eID="gen25780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against--</hi>or "over." <div eID="gen25781" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a4d277685b179fb191eb30087b3c3c7021a783d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13486"/><div sID="gen25782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13486"/><hi type="bold">2. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these--</hi>The other Evangelists enumerate the twelve in immediate connection with their appointment (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.13-Mark.3.19">Mr 3:13-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.13-Luke.6.16">Lu 6:13-16</reference>). But our Evangelist, not intending to record the appointment, but only the Mission of the Twelve, gives their names here. And as in the Acts (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.13">Ac 1:13</reference>) we have a list of the Eleven who met daily in the upper room with the other disciples after their Master's ascension until the day of Pentecost, we have four catalogues in all for comparison.<div eID="gen25782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The first, Simon, who is called Peter--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.1.42">Joh 1:42</reference>).<div eID="gen25783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother--</hi>named after James, as the younger of the two. <div eID="gen25784" type="x-p"/>
entries.709976846a6387262621c015e321b2288bd21d0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13487"/><div sID="gen25785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13487"/><hi type="bold">3. Philip and Bartholomew--</hi>That this person is the same with "Nathanael of Cana in Galilee" is justly concluded for the three following reasons: First, because Bartholomew is not so properly an individual's name as a family surname; next, because not only in this list, but in Mark's and Luke's (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.18">Mr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.14">Lu 6:14</reference>), he follows the name of "Philip," who was the instrument of bringing Nathanael first to Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.1.45">Joh 1:45</reference>); and again, when our Lord, after His resurrection, appeared at the Sea of Tiberias, "Nathanael of Cana in Galilee" is mentioned along with six others, all of them apostles, as being present (<reference osisRef="John.21.2">Joh 21:2</reference>).<div eID="gen25785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Matthew the publican--</hi>In none of the four lists of the Twelve is this apostle so branded but in his own, as if he would have all to know how deep a debtor he had been to his Lord. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.3">Mt 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen25786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">James the son of Alphaeus--</hi>the same person apparently who is called Cleopas or Clopas (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.18">Lu 24:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference>); and, as he was the husband of Mary, sister to the Virgin, James the Less must have been our Lord's cousin.<div eID="gen25787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus--</hi>the same, without doubt, as "Judas the brother of James," mentioned in both the lists of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.16">Lu 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.13">Ac 1:13</reference>), while no one of the name of Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus is so. It is he who in John (<reference osisRef="John.14.22">Joh 14:22</reference>) is sweetly called "Judas, not Iscariot." That he was the author of the Catholic Epistle of "Jude," and not "the Lord's brother" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.55">Mt 13:55</reference>), unless these be the same, is most likely. <div eID="gen25788" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f2ca055991254944ba9970c7847a58db4a5232a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13488"/><div sID="gen25789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13488"/><hi type="bold">4. Simon the Canaanite--</hi>rather "Kananite," but better still, "the Zealot," as he is called in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.15">Lu 6:15</reference>, where the original term should not have been retained as in our version ("Simon, called Zelotes"), but rendered "Simon, called the Zealot." The word "Kananite" is just the Aramaic, or Syro-Chaldaic, term for "Zealot." Probably before his acquaintance with Jesus, he belonged to the sect of the Zealots, who bound themselves, as a sort of voluntary ecclesiastical police, to see that the law was not broken with impunity.<div eID="gen25789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Judas Iscariot--</hi>that is, Judas of Kerioth, a town of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.25">Jos 15:25</reference>); so called to distinguish him from "Judas the brother of James" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.16">Lu 6:16</reference>).<div eID="gen25790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who also betrayed him--</hi>a note of infamy attached to his name in all the catalogues of the Twelve.<div eID="gen25791" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.42">Mt 10:5-42</reference>. The Twelve Receive Their Instructions.</title> <div sID="gen25792" type="x-p"/> This directory divides itself into three distinct parts. The first part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">Mt 10:5-15</reference>) contains directions for the brief and temporary mission on which they were now going forth, with respect to the places they were to go to, the works they were to do, the message they were to bear, and the manner in which they were to conduct themselves. The second part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16-Matt.10.23">Mt 10:16-23</reference>) contains directions of no such limited and temporary nature, but opens out into the permanent exercise of the Gospel ministry. The third part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24-Matt.10.42">Mt 10:24-42</reference>) is of wider application still, reaching not only to the ministry of the Gospel in every age, but to the service of Christ in the widest sense. It is a strong confirmation of this threefold division, that each part closes with the words, "Verily I SAY UNTO YOU" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.15">Mt 10:15</reference>, 23, 42).<div eID="gen25792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25793" type="x-p"/> Directions for the Present Mission (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">Mt 10:5-15</reference>). <div eID="gen25793" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a9b4bb9727833797cb4c30e8b4b40bd5141a02a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13489"/><div sID="gen25794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13489"/><hi type="bold">5. These twelve Jesus sent forth, and commanded them, saying, Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not--</hi>The Samaritans were Gentiles by blood; but being the descendants of those whom the king of Assyria had transported from the East to supply the place of the ten tribes carried captive, they had adopted the religion of the Jews, though with admixtures of their own: and, as the nearest neighbors of the Jews, they occupied a place intermediate between them and the Gentiles. Accordingly, when this prohibition was to be taken off, on the effusion of the Spirit at Pentecost, the apostles were told that they should be Christ's witnesses first "in Jerusalem, and in all Judea," then "in Samaria," and lastly, "unto the uttermost part of the earth" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Ac 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen25794" type="x-p"/>
entries.993ee87090db6843d833bb9ef166cf1ab651b21d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13490"/><div sID="gen25795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13490"/><hi type="bold">6. But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel--</hi>Until Christ's death, which broke down the middle wall of partition (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>), the Gospel commission was to the Jews only, who, though the visible people of God, were "lost sheep," not merely in the sense which all sinners are (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">Is 53:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.25">1Pe 2:25</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Luke.19.10">Lu 19:10</reference>), but as abandoned and left to wander from the right way by faithless shepherds (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jr 50:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2-Ezek.34.6">Eze 34:2-6</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen25795" type="x-p"/>
entries.d85673079babf381ca078dba80841afb66d3a165: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13491"/><div sID="gen25796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13491"/><hi type="bold">7. And as ye go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.2">Mt 3:2</reference>). <div eID="gen25796" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1dce6e9f8d54296fe6c3745e5736b30cec9ece9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13492"/><div sID="gen25797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13492"/><hi type="bold">8. Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils--</hi>(The italicized clause--"raise the dead"--is wanting in many manuscripts). Here we have the first communication of supernatural power by Christ Himself to His followers--thus anticipating the gifts of Pentecost. And right royally does He dispense it.<div eID="gen25797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">freely ye have received, freely give--</hi>Divine saying, divinely said! <hi type="bold">(Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.15.10">De 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.6">Ac 3:6</reference>)--</hi>an apple of gold in a setting of silver (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.11">Pr 25:11</reference>). It reminds us of that other golden saying of our Lord, rescued from oblivion by Paul, "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Ac 20:35</reference>). Who can estimate what the world owes to such sayings, and with what beautiful foliage and rich fruit such seeds have covered, and will yet cover, this earth! <div eID="gen25798" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f635cd1a50738c028a330bd6ddb11fcf0bf4f6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13493"/><div sID="gen25799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13493"/><hi type="bold">9. Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses--</hi>"for" your purses; literally, "your belts," in which they kept their money. <div eID="gen25799" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc7496c95108fd8540c54a3f47e16be7676ae10a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13494"/><div sID="gen25800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13494"/><hi type="bold">10. Nor scrip for your journey--</hi>the bag used by travellers for holding provisions.<div eID="gen25800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither two coats--</hi>or tunics, worn next the skin. The meaning is, Take no change of dress, no additional articles.<div eID="gen25801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shoes--</hi>that is, change of them.<div eID="gen25802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor yet staves--</hi>The received text here has "a staff," but our version follows another reading, "staves," which is found in the received text of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.3">Lu 9:3</reference>). The true reading, however, evidently is "a staff"--meaning, that they were not to procure even that much expressly for this missionary journey, but to go with what they had. No doubt it was the misunderstanding of this that gave rise to the reading "staves" in so many manuscripts Even if this reading were genuine, it could not mean "more than one"; for who, as Alford well asks, would think of taking a spare staff?<div eID="gen25803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the workman is worthy of his meat--</hi>his "food" or "maintenance"; a principle which, being universally recognized in secular affairs, is here authoritatively applied to the services of the Lord's workmen, and by Paul repeatedly and touchingly employed in his appeals to the churches (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.27">Ro 15:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">1Co 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>), and once as "scripture" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">1Ti 5:18</reference>). <div eID="gen25804" type="x-p"/>
entries.5349d8c22ab8ee9b0ad5de032db34545a4601860: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13495"/><div sID="gen25805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13495"/><hi type="bold">11. And into whatsoever city or town--</hi>town or village.<div eID="gen25805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall enter inquire--</hi>carefully.<div eID="gen25806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who in it is worthy--</hi>or "meet" to entertain such messengers; not in point of rank, of course, but of congenial disposition.<div eID="gen25807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and there abide till ye go thence--</hi>not shifting about, as if discontented, but returning the welcome given with a courteous, contented, accommodating disposition. <div eID="gen25808" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f349512119c598c8f2e5f39096d96df5f037ef4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13496"/><div sID="gen25809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13496"/><hi type="bold">12. And when ye come into an house--</hi>or "the house," but it means not the worthy house, but the house ye first enter, to try if it be worthy.<div eID="gen25809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salute it--</hi>show it the usual civilities. <div eID="gen25810" type="x-p"/>
entries.73e24931dfec32cb1cd3dc5488c174d7c3235a28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13497"/><div sID="gen25811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13497"/><hi type="bold">13. And if the house be worthy--</hi>showing this by giving you a welcome.<div eID="gen25811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let your peace come upon it--</hi>This is best explained by the injunction to the Seventy, "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house" (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.5">Lu 10:5</reference>). This was the ancient salutation of the East, and it prevails to this day. But from the lips of Christ and His messengers, it means something far higher, both in the gift and the giving of it, than in the current salutation. (See on <reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>).<div eID="gen25812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but if it be not worthy, let your peace return to you--</hi>If your peace finds a shut, instead of an open, door in the heart of any household, take it back to yourselves, who know how to value it; and it will taste the sweeter to you for having been offered, even though rejected. <div eID="gen25813" type="x-p"/>
entries.f27367e84ad1208e98ccfc96014c91fa01a4d7ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13498"/><div sID="gen25814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13498"/><hi type="bold">14. And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city--</hi>for possibly a whole town might not furnish one "worthy."<div eID="gen25814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake off the dust of your feet--</hi>"for a testimony against them," as Mark and Luke add (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.11">Mr 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.11">Lu 10:11</reference>). By this symbolical action they vividly shook themselves from all connection with such, and all responsibility for the guilt of rejecting them and their message. Such symbolical actions were common in ancient times, even among others than the Jews, as strikingly appears in Pilate (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.24">Mt 27:24</reference>). And even to this day it prevails in the East. <div eID="gen25815" type="x-p"/>
entries.df48e0442f25c00e2340daa5e923074bc0f14a24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13499"/><div sID="gen25816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13499"/><hi type="bold">15. Verily I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable--</hi>more bearable.<div eID="gen25816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment, than for that city--</hi>Those Cities of the Plain, which were given to the flames for their loathsome impurities, shall be treated as less criminal, we are here taught, than those places which, though morally respectable, reject the Gospel message and affront those that bear it.<div eID="gen25817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25818" type="x-p"/> Directions for the Future and Permanent Exercise of the Christian Ministry (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16-Matt.10.23">Mt 10:16-23</reference>). <div eID="gen25818" type="x-p"/>
entries.4dd602cac6bdcc7a09a73c332c679e06b3c6cfc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13500"/><div sID="gen25819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13500"/><hi type="bold">16. Behold, I send you forth--</hi>The "I" here is emphatic, holding up Himself as the Fountain of the Gospel ministry, as He is also the Great Burden of it.<div eID="gen25819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as sheep--</hi>defenseless.<div eID="gen25820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of wolves--</hi>ready to make a prey of you (<reference osisRef="John.10.12">Joh 10:12</reference>). To be left exposed, as sheep to wolves, would have been startling enough; but that the sheep should be sent among the wolves would sound strange indeed. No wonder this announcement begins with the exclamation, "Behold."<div eID="gen25821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves--</hi>Wonderful combination this! Alone, the wisdom of the serpent is mere cunning, and the harmlessness of the dove little better than weakness: but in combination, the wisdom of the serpent would save them from unnecessary exposure to danger; the harmlessness of the dove, from sinful expedients to escape it. In the apostolic age of Christianity, how harmoniously were these qualities displayed! Instead of the fanatical thirst for martyrdom, to which a later age gave birth, there was a manly combination of unflinching zeal and calm discretion, before which nothing was able to stand. <div eID="gen25822" type="x-p"/>
entries.a144910cfec02ccd882e0deb553624efa172615a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13501"/><div sID="gen25823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13501"/><hi type="bold">17. But beware of men; for they will deliver you up to the councils--</hi>the local courts, used here for civil magistrates in general.<div eID="gen25823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they will scourge you in their synagogues--</hi>By this is meant persecution at the hands of the ecclesiastics. <div eID="gen25824" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb3d266a25821954762350ccfc900e913af22187: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13502"/><div sID="gen25825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13502"/><hi type="bold">18. And ye shall be brought before governors--</hi>provincial rulers.<div eID="gen25825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and kings--</hi>the highest tribunals.<div eID="gen25826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for my sake, for a testimony against them--</hi>rather, "to them," in order to bear testimony to the truth and its glorious effects.<div eID="gen25827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Gentiles--</hi>"to the Gentiles"; a hint that their message would not long be confined to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. The Acts of the Apostles are the best commentary on these warnings. <div eID="gen25828" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7c25f948953bb9c5bf454025e57d72036181f78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13503"/><div sID="gen25829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13503"/><hi type="bold">19. But when they deliver you up, take no thought--</hi>be not solicitous or anxious. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Mt 6:25</reference>).<div eID="gen25829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how or what ye shall speak--</hi>that is, either in what manner ye shall make your defense, or of what matter it shall consist.<div eID="gen25830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Exod.4.12">Ex 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.7">Jr 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen25831" type="x-p"/>
entries.aaf700f0a69d99369e25667d15bc493ddb3f8f0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13504"/><div sID="gen25832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13504"/><hi type="bold">20. For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you--</hi>How remarkably this has been verified, the whole history of persecution thrillingly proclaims--from the Acts of the Apostles to the latest martyrology. <div eID="gen25832" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3e524a44364bbe0ac863ee0369de1ecc9578309: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13505"/><div sID="gen25833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13505"/><hi type="bold">21. And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child: and the children shall rise up against their parents, and cause them to be put to death--</hi>for example, by lodging information against them with the authorities. The deep and virulent hostility of the old nature and life to the new--as of Belial to Christ--was to issue in awful wrenches of the dearest ties; and the disciples, in the prospect of their cause and themselves being launched upon society, are here prepared for the worst. <div eID="gen25833" type="x-p"/>
entries.156de23aa2df59fc7ce65be8bc1bd8ccdb33bbe8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13506"/><div sID="gen25834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13506"/><hi type="bold">22. And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake--</hi>The universality of this hatred would make it evident to them, that since it would not be owing to any temporary excitement, local virulence, or personal prejudice, on the part of their enemies, so no amount of discretion on their part, consistent with entire fidelity to the truth, would avail to stifle that enmity--though it might soften its violence, and in some cases avert the outward manifestations of it.<div eID="gen25834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he that endureth to the end shall be saved--</hi>a great saying, repeated, in connection with similar warnings, in the prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.13">Mt 24:13</reference>); and often reiterated by the apostle as a warning against "drawing back unto perdition" (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">He 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">6:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">10:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">26-29</reference>, 38, 39, &c.). As "drawing back unto perdition" is merely the palpable evidence of the want of "root" from the first in the Christian profession (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.13">Lu 8:13</reference>), so "enduring to the end" is just the proper evidence of its reality and solidity. <div eID="gen25835" type="x-p"/>
entries.84e37e0725ac1bab5da23cc85d0cabb0e39d463c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13507"/><div sID="gen25836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13507"/><hi type="bold">23. But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another--</hi>"into the other." This, though applicable to all time, and exemplified by our Lord Himself once and again, had special reference to the brief opportunities which Israel was to have of "knowing the time of His visitations."<div eID="gen25836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for verily I say unto you--</hi>what will startle you, but at the same time show you the solemnity of your mission, and the need of economizing the time for it.<div eID="gen25837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye shall not have gone over--</hi>Ye shall in nowise have completed.<div eID="gen25838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come--</hi>To understand this--as Lange and others do--in the first instance, of Christ's own peregrinations, as if He had said, "Waste not your time upon hostile places, for I Myself will be after you ere your work be over"--seems almost trifling. "The coming of the Son of man" has a fixed doctrinal sense, here referring immediately to the crisis of Israel's history as the visible kingdom of God, when Christ was to come and judge it; when "the wrath would come upon it to the uttermost"; and when, on the ruins of Jerusalem and the old economy, He would establish His own kingdom. This, in the uniform language of Scripture, is more immediately "the coming of the Son of man," "the day of vengeance of our God" (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.28">Mt 16:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.27">24:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.34">34</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7-Jas.5.9">Jas 5:7-9</reference>)--but only as being such a lively anticipation of His second coming for vengeance and deliverance. So understood, it is parallel with <reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Mt 24:14</reference> (on which see).<div eID="gen25839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25840" type="x-p"/> Directions for the Service of Christ in Its Widest Sense (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24-Matt.10.42">Mt 10:24-42</reference>). <div eID="gen25840" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf97406449c93dba678b54989af04aad910d89a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13508"/><div sID="gen25841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13508"/><hi type="bold">24. The disciple is not above his master--</hi>teacher.<div eID="gen25841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor the servant above his lord--</hi>another maxim which our Lord repeats in various connections (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.40">Lu 6:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.13.16">Joh 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.20">15:20</reference>). <div eID="gen25842" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dfe81f74eeba3d0fcdcdab0712e28fbb3b43162: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13509"/><div sID="gen25843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13509"/><hi type="bold">25. It is enough for the disciple that he be as his master, and the servant as his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub--</hi>All the Greek manuscripts, write "Beelzebul," which undoubtedly is the right form of this word. The other reading came in no doubt from the Old Testament "Baalzebub," the god of Ekron (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.2">2Ki 1:2</reference>), which it was designed to express. As all idolatry was regarded as devil worship (<reference osisRef="Lev.17.7">Le 17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">De 32:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.37">Psa 106:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.20">1Co 10:20</reference>), so there seems to have been something peculiarly satanic about the worship of this hateful god, which caused his name to be a synonym of Satan. Though we nowhere read that our Lord was actually called "Beelzebul," He was charged with being in league with Satan under that hateful name (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.24">Mt 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.26">26</reference>), and more than once Himself was charged with "having a devil" or "demon" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.30">Mr 3:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.20">Joh 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.48">8:48</reference>). Here it is used to denote the most opprobrious language which could be applied by one to another.<div eID="gen25843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how much more shall they call them of his household--</hi>"the inmates." Three relations in which Christ stands to His people are here mentioned: He is their Teacher--they His disciples; He is their Lord--they His servants; He is the Master of the household--they its inmates. In all these relations, He says here, He and they are so bound up together that they cannot look to fare better than He, and should think it enough if they fare no worse. <div eID="gen25844" type="x-p"/>
entries.84c7ef0874ad42ec78894936c77dd7bfc7f1f6cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13510"/><div sID="gen25845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13510"/><hi type="bold">26. Fear them not therefore: for there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known--</hi>that is, There is no use, and no need, of concealing anything; right and wrong, truth and error, are about to come into open and deadly collision; and the day is coming when all hidden things shall be disclosed, everything seen as it is, and every one have his due (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:5</reference>). <div eID="gen25845" type="x-p"/>
entries.22039338d6dd5f9f02242735075dacfacd40c2b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13511"/><div sID="gen25846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13511"/><hi type="bold">27. What I tell you in darkness--</hi>in the privacy of a teaching for which men are not yet ripe.<div eID="gen25846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that speak ye in the light--</hi>for when ye go forth all will be ready.<div eID="gen25847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops--</hi>Give free and fearless utterance to all that I have taught you while yet with you. Objection: But this may cost us our life? Answer: It may, but there their power ends: <div eID="gen25848" type="x-p"/>
entries.46cef255cbdd1b4b968879a4cca91f61499e9513: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13512"/><div sID="gen25849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13512"/><hi type="bold">28. And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Lu 12:4</reference>, "and after that have no more that they can do."<div eID="gen25849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but rather fear him--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.5">Lu 12:5</reference>) this is peculiarly solemn, "I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear," even Him<div eID="gen25850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell--</hi>A decisive proof this that there is a hell for the body as well as the soul in the eternal world; in other words, that the torment that awaits the lost will have elements of suffering adapted to the material as well as the spiritual part of our nature, both of which, we are assured, will exist for ever. In the corresponding warning contained in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Lu 12:4</reference>), Jesus calls His disciples "My friends," as if He had felt that such sufferings constituted a bond of peculiar tenderness between Him and them. <div eID="gen25851" type="x-p"/>
entries.077ddd2fd0f2d75d8621c520e7ad5dbf13e58daf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13513"/><div sID="gen25852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13513"/><hi type="bold">29. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing?--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.6">Lu 12:6</reference>) it is "five sparrows for two farthings"; so that, if the purchaser took two farthings' worth, he got one in addition--of such small value were they.<div eID="gen25852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and one of them shall not fall on the ground--</hi>exhausted or killed<div eID="gen25853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without your Father--</hi>"Not one of them is forgotten before God," as it is in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.6">Lu 12:6</reference>). <div eID="gen25854" type="x-p"/>
entries.badebd5a988b6fdd228f106a49c4502e630f918c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13514"/><div sID="gen25855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13514"/><hi type="bold">30. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered--</hi>See <reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">Lu 21:18</reference> (and compare for the language <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.27.34">Ac 27:34</reference>). <div eID="gen25855" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e9228b03388efd667860a2f71a3281f2327e672: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13515"/><div sID="gen25856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13515"/><hi type="bold">31. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows--</hi>Was ever language of such simplicity felt to carry such weight as this does? But here lies much of the charm and power of our Lord's teaching. <div eID="gen25856" type="x-p"/>
entries.e91c2807f4b92c17b2bd95a6a7bd96c782f0c72a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13516"/><div sID="gen25857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13516"/><hi type="bold">32. Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men--</hi>despising the shame.<div eID="gen25857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven--</hi>I will not be ashamed of him, but will own him before the most august of all assemblies. <div eID="gen25858" type="x-p"/>
entries.073be178754f4adf7929c54dd691c8356f4e95e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13517"/><div sID="gen25859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13517"/><hi type="bold">33. But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven--</hi>before that same assembly: "He shall have from Me his own treatment of Me on the earth." (But see on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.27">Mt 16:27</reference>). <div eID="gen25859" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a8791796d1aa2a4fe98f01abe6ddc561c7a5ebd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13518"/><div sID="gen25860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13518"/><hi type="bold">34. Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword--</hi>strife, discord, conflict; deadly opposition between eternally hostile principles, penetrating into and rending asunder the dearest ties. <div eID="gen25860" type="x-p"/>
entries.06af55fe7039292b8974affa9159fe822e0b8081: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13519"/><div sID="gen25861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13519"/><hi type="bold">35. For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.12.51-Luke.12.53">Lu 12:51-53</reference>). <div eID="gen25861" type="x-p"/>
entries.692ee4987e33e5aefc2764b757bb7d3ec7bdcbf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13520"/><div sID="gen25862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13520"/><hi type="bold">36.
